items.question: How do you envision humanity’s future evolution?
items.object: Humanity’s future evolution
items.answer: I think the future will be a new species—just one that is extremely intelligent and highly capable. When we look at people from 30,000 years ago, would you say they were the same species? I think they were very different. The Upper Cave people 30,000 years ago already had tools; in the Stone Age they had fire, but their tools were very primitive. Today, we have mobile phones, computers, and the internet. But in another hundred years, people will look at today’s phones and internet the way we look at the fire and stone tools of 30,000 years ago. And the pace of evolution will become very fast.

items.question: How do you understand the change in artificial intelligence from your work in China in 1998 to its development over the past decade?
items.object: AI’s development from the late 1990s to the past decade
items.answer: What we were doing then was all related to artificial intelligence, but no one called it artificial intelligence. At that time, AI was basically in a period of hibernation. In 1998, Kai-Fu was working on speech recognition and synthesis; I was doing video compression; Dongjiang was doing imaging; Shen Xiangyang was doing computer vision and graphics; Professor Huang was doing NLP, natural language. Looking at it now, all of these things ultimately converged into AI, but at the time we did not call them AI. AI’s real development has happened over the past decade, when it truly became a useful science. Before that it was still an exploratory period. It also brought together a broad convergence of computer vision, video, natural language, speech, and statistical learning itself.

items.question: How did you assess the challenge of building a world-class computer research institute in China when Microsoft Research China was founded?
items.object: Building a world-class computer research institute in China when Microsoft Research China was founded
items.answer: The biggest challenge was whether it was possible to build a world-class research institute in China, because none existed then. Think about it: 30 years ago, most universities in China were far behind the United States in research capability. That included the PhD students we trained—the methods of doing research, the level of research, and research achievements. There was still a big gap with the United States, unlike today. So the greatest challenge then was whether we could build a world-class computer research institute in China. And many people had question marks. Some American colleagues did not necessarily have confidence in it. But I think the few of us definitely did; we believed it could be done. Microsoft also had confidence in us. Gates also had confidence in us.

items.question: How do you judge whether a research institute has become world-class?
items.object: Recognizing a world-class research institute
items.answer: Our institute did not really have quantitative metrics. Our goal was simply to become a world-class computer research institute. That was it. And this itself is hard to quantify. I remember chatting with Kai-Fu, and also with one of our advisers, George Ratti, a Turing Award winner, about how to measure it—how would we know we were first-rate? He said: when you no longer ask or talk about that question, you have become first-rate. In other words, you just naturally feel it. I understood that more deeply later. After ChatGPT came out, within half an hour of using it, my first impression was: ChatGPT has passed the Turing test. In the past, we often asked when we would know that the Turing test had been passed. And I think it was Jim Gray, also a Turing Award winner, who said: when you pass it, you know. So you know; you do not need to measure it.

items.question: How do you see the choice of research directions for an AI institute today compared with when you were building Microsoft Research in China?
items.object: Choosing research directions for an AI research institute
items.answer: In some areas, for example, we wanted to do something but could not find the right people—could not find leaders in that field—then we could not get it going, right? items.question: How do you understand the relationship between information intelligence, physical intelligence, and biological intelligence in the new generation of AI?
items.object: Information, physical, and biological intelligence as the three domains of a new generation of AI
items.answer: Let me back up a bit. I have always believed that this new intelligence—this new generation of AI—is information intelligence plus physical intelligence plus biological intelligence. I have been saying this for ten years. At Davos and at these conferences, I have kept making one point: information intelligence is simple; it is things like ChatGPT today. All our text, images, and videos—the intelligence of the information world. Physical intelligence is applying it to, for example, autonomous vehicles, robots, and what people now call embodied intelligence. Applying it to physical infrastructure—that is physical intelligence. IoT is included as well: intelligence in the physical world. Then there is intelligence in the biological world: applying AI to things like brain-computer interfaces. Like Elon Musk’s Neuralink. And connecting it to organisms and living bodies, including medical and surgical robots and new-drug development. These are three different domains. They are of course interconnected, but still distinct fields. I believe that within five years, in the information domain—in information intelligence—we can pass the Turing test and reach the level of AGI.

They can solve problems, invent new formulas, write good articles, paint, and compose poetry. That is a person’s basic IQ, put simply. Information intelligence is like the IQ of our brains. But even if you read all the books about swimming, you still cannot swim; you have to swim in order to swim, right? That is the physical world: you have to engage with it. items.question: Why do you expect autonomous driving to be deployed before general-purpose robots?
items.object: Autonomous driving as an early deployment of physical intelligence
items.answer: I personally think the first deployment will be driverless driving, because autonomous driving operates in a relatively controllable setting. Robotics is an open problem; autonomous driving is a closed problem. I only need to do this one task and can do it very well. For driving, unlike with a robot, I do not need common sense, understanding of human behavior, or the ability to handle many complex and differing environments. You could say autonomous driving is a driving robot, a robot in a vertical domain. A robot for a special scenario. But it only does this one thing. If you drive well, as a driver, you do not need to know how to write poetry. You do not need a very high IQ, you do not need to know how to sing, and you do not need to understand biology. You just need to do that one thing well. You do not need to know how to weld in a factory. But humanoid robots, or general-purpose robots, have more requirements.

items.answer: I think there is a difference between humanoid and non-humanoid robots. items.question: Why do you see foundation models as a major catalyst for progress in autonomous driving?
items.object: Foundation models as a catalyst for autonomous driving
items.answer: I think people saw the dawn this year. A major catalyst was the foundation model. Driverless driving has had several major problems over the years. First, insufficient data—mainly a lack of testing data. Second, many corner cases. There are many scenarios related to safety that you do not encounter. New problems arise in testing, and generalization is relatively poor. Third, the AI models used to be one model for maps, one for vision, one model for language processing. Radar and lidar each had their own models; they were all vertical and fragmented. Fragmented models had to be assembled, then perception had to happen, then fusion, then planning and decision-making. Everything was done piece by piece. There were many rules, AI algorithms, neural-network algorithms, and many fixed rules all put together in a very messy way. After foundation models came out, they helped us rapidly—not completely solve these problems, I would not say that—but accelerate progress on these three major challenges. First, if data is insufficient, generative AI can generate a great deal of data in addition to real data, making simulation much faster. Second, many scenarios are missing, but foundation models themselves have strong generalization capability—common sense. Foundation models have common sense, and can also learn common sense through simulation, so they can relatively easily address many things they have not encountered. Third, and very importantly, you now do end-to-end. I no longer care about all those individual models; I put the boxes together, with one input and one output, right? At most, you use some rules as a fallback. So these three major challenges are not completely solved, I would not say that, but greatly alleviated; they have rapidly and substantially accelerated autonomous-driving development.

items.question: How do you see foundation models changing the way robots acquire common sense?

items.answer: Driving is simple in the sense that you just drive; cars are fixed. Driving itself must be very precise and safe, but it is one thing to do well. Things like that—the small details. You cannot set a new algorithm for every one. Early on, we used rules. Now we do not: it sees something and learns it. After learning, it can open anything you put in front of it. It knows how large an item is needed; for example, if you bring tea, it knows it is hot and will be careful when handing it to you. It learns things like that—what we call common sense. Where does that common sense come from? From foundation models. You do not need to teach it every single thing. In the past there were rules—how many rules would that take? Now you do not need to teach it. Once it learns, it has the opportunity to reason by itself. Like a person: if it knows you and knows you like bananas, it may find a banana in the room and bring it to you. Or if you do not eat lamb, when ordering food it will not order lamb for you. Such things become common; it need not remember every time. Like a person, it understands you and knows basic common sense.

items.object: The book “Search Memory” and its account of memory
items.answer: I think the most important kind of intelligence for people today is memory. Memory is divided into several levels: innate genetic memory—that is, genes, genetic memory; then there is short-term memory; and then there is long-term memory. And learning is actually about taking these memories—how you remember them. Knowledge, for example, some long-term kind of knowledge in the brain—the cerebral cortex. AI today does not really understand this. At present, AI's abstraction of knowledge—so I think this is particularly well written. How we humans remember things, including, for example, older people with amnesia—you find that it is all about their brain's memory. For example, the hippocampus starts to shrink and atrophy, and then a person's so-called intelligence is gone. So memory is especially important. Right now, AI's memory is still not very good, or it is not divided in this way. In fact, I think the book is very well written.
